verdict.reasoning: Patient reports anxiety about leaving the house, sleep disturbance, and palpitations: "I've been feeling really anxious... I just get really nervous every morning about leaving the house" and "it's really impacting on... my sleep" and describes "my heart kind of racing".

Duration and trigger: "I think I would say maybe about two months or so... that's probably coincides with me starting a new job... quite stressful" and job is at "a fashion retailer in the head office team."
Dreading work and worry about performance: "I just really dread going there... really worried about whether I'm doing well or not."
Impact on sleep and daily life: "it's really impacting on like on the rest of my life, like my sleep" and later describes low enjoyment and fatigue affecting activities.
Bedtime and sleep onset difficulty: Doctor asks what time she goes to bed and she responds, "About 10, 11" and then, "Not for ages. I'm lying awake all night."
Non-restorative sleep and duration: "I feel like I'm... even when I'm in sleep, it's such a shallow sleep. But maybe three, four hours I'm getting now."

Waking with racing heart/fear of being late: "I find my heart kind of racing, and then I'm just, like, panicking that I'm going to be late... I find myself waking up before [the alarm] because... my heart is racing."

Irregular fast palpitations and duration: "just a constant, like, rapid heart beating" and when asked if regular or irregular, patient says, "Irregular, I think" and episodes last "a couple of minutes" to "like, 10 minutes."

Chest discomfort with palpitations: In response to chest pain, patient says, "No. Well, yeah, it's painful when the heart. When my heart is being fat, but yeah," indicating discomfort when heart is racing.

Low mood and reduced interest: "I'm finding now that I'm just. I find no enjoyment at all" and "anything that previously was really fun is just not enjoyable... it's just the kind of like constant feeling of just being a bit down, a bit unhappy."
Low energy: "how's your energy level in the daytime?" Patient: "It's just really, really low."

Social withdrawal: On friends, patient says, "I avoid them in so much that I feel like I'm... I know that I'm not going to have fun because I don't want to go out and do things that I would normally have done."

Reduced hobbies/exercise: "everything that I had previously been doing has been just difficult to continue with... I did used to like to go running and to play tennis... but now... I'm not going out to do that quite so much."

Difficulty with evening activities: "right now I'm working so late... I don't really get much time for myself. But when I do want to go out or be friends or just relax, it seems quite difficult to do that."
Denies suicidal thoughts: "I haven't had any suicidal thoughts or any thoughts that have been that extreme."
No vitals/exam/labs are mentioned anywhere in the transcript, so stating they are not documented is accurate.
There is no discussion of past medical conditions in the transcript; thus past medical history is not documented.
No current medications are asked about or listed in the transcript; therefore they are not documented.
Allergies are never mentioned in the transcript; stating they are not documented reflects the transcript.
Patient reports family history: "I talked to my mum because she also suffers from, or she's suffered from like depression in the past," so some family history is documented.
Employment: "I work for a fashion retailer in the head office team" and the context of ongoing full-time work is clear.
Heavier alcohol use on weekends: "probably quite a lot on the Friday or Saturday day... maybe like, I probably go over my limit just on those days anyway."
Occasional smoking: "Do you smoke... ?" Patient: "I try not to smoke, but I do occasionally."
No illicit drug use: In response to drugs, patient says, "I don't take them."
Living situation: "I live with my parents. With my parents."
Supportive family: "I have. I have a good support system. Like, I do have a good family and stuff."

Clinician frames anxiety disorder with somatic symptoms and impairment: She has anxiety linked to work with "palpitations" and "sleep patterns" issues, plus impact on work and social activities; doctor discusses anxiety treatment and says "Some people with anxiety, they do need to take medication" indicating assessment of an anxiety disorder related to work stress and withdrawal.

Insomnia with daytime fatigue and anhedonia: Patient reports "maybe three, four hours" shallow sleep, "really, really low" energy, and "I find no enjoyment at all"; clinician mentions helping with "your sleep patterns."

Depressed mood in anxiety context without suicidality: Patient reports feeling "a bit down, a bit unhappy" and loss of enjoyment, and clearly states "I haven't had any suicidal thoughts"; anxiety is primary focus.

Clinician links palpitations to anxiety but plans medical evaluation: "In terms of palpitations, it is most likely to be associated with anxiety, but it's probably worth having a couple of basic blood tests just to make sure that there's not something triggering that off."
New job as occupational stressor: Patient ties onset to starting new job and calls it "really stressful"; clinician repeatedly discusses anxiety in relation to work stress.
Self-referral to NHS talking therapies: "you can self refer via the NHS for what we call like talking therapy, which is a type of behavioral therapy... So I can send you the link for that."

Online resources and review if worse/no improvement: "In the meantime... There are some online resources that are really helpful... if you're feeling like it's not helping at all or your anxiety is getting worse... then it's important for you to give us a call back and just discuss that further."

Clinician mentions general sleep advice but not specific sleep hygiene components: "I'll put some more information on your notes about helping with your sleep patterns and things like that." There is no explicit mention of caffeine, screen use, or detailed schedule strategies.
Basic blood tests for palpitations: "it's probably worth having a couple of basic blood tests just to make sure that there's not something triggering that off."
Follow-up in about a week after tests: "arranging a GP follow up a week after you've had the test so we can just go through the results with you."

Medication as future option but not started: "Some people with anxiety, they do need to take medication to control that, but that's not something that we suggest in the first instance." No prescription is given in the transcript.
The transcript does not mention advice about chest pain, fainting, or increasing suicidality as reasons to contact GP/urgent care; this safety-netting detail is not present.
Although alcohol use is discussed, there is no documented advice about reducing alcohol or providing support resources; this is new content.
Clinician does not explicitly encourage maintaining social contact or graded re-engagement in activities; this is inferred planning not stated.
Information to be sent/attached: "I can send you the link for that" and "I'll put some more information on your notes about helping with your sleep patterns and things like that."
Follow-up timing: "arranging a GP follow up a week after you've had the test so we can just go through the results with you."
The instruction to seek urgent or GP review for chest pain, fainting, or increasing suicidality is not mentioned in the transcript.
Palpitations characteristics come from patient history, not an objective physical exam; the transcript has no exam findings. Thus describing them as a physical exam observation is additional.

Sleep disturbance description matches: difficulty falling asleep ("Not for ages. I'm lying awake all night"), short duration ("maybe three, four hours"), and awakening with anxiety/palpitations ("I find my heart kind of racing... I find myself waking up before [the alarm]").

Mood observations align with reported symptoms: distress noted by doctor, patient describes being "pretty much down," "a bit down, a bit unhappy," "I find no enjoyment at all," and "really, really low" energy.
Functional impairment: patient avoids friends and activities—"I avoid them... I don't want to go out" and reduced running/tennis—indicating social withdrawal and reduced engagement.
Substance use: "probably quite a lot on the Friday or Saturday day... probably go over my limit" plus "I try not to smoke, but I do occasionally" and "I don't take them" (re drugs).
Cardiovascular ROS: palpitations and discomfort—"just a constant, like, rapid heart beating" and chest pain response: "Well, yeah, it's painful when... my heart is being fat."

Sleep ROS: difficulty falling asleep ("Not for ages. I'm lying awake all night"), non-restorative short sleep ("shallow sleep" and "three, four hours"), and awakenings with racing heart and fear of lateness.

Psych ROS: anxiety (throughout), low mood ("a bit down, a bit unhappy"), anhedonia ("I find no enjoyment at all"), reduced interest, low energy ("really, really low"), and explicit denial of suicidal thoughts.
